'''''Brassica rapa''''' is an annual to biennial [[plant]] species native to [[Eurasia]] that is from the [[Brassicaceae]] family. The ''B. rapa'' subspecies ''oleifera'' is an [[oilseed]] commonly known as '''turnip rape''', '''field mustard''', '''bird's rape''', and '''keblock'''.<ref name=USDA>{{GRIN | ''Brassica rapa'' subsp. ''oleifera'' | 319648 | access-date = 13 April 2013}}</ref><ref name=EOL>{{cite web|title=''Brassica rapa'' subsp. oleifera|url=http://eol.org/pages/10451733/overview|work=Turnip Rape|publisher=EOL|access-date=13 April 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |publisher=Cambridge |location=Cambridge |year=1997 |title=New Flora of the British Isles|author=Clive Stace|author-link = Clive A. Stace|isbn=978-0-521-58935-2}}</ref>

It has been widely cultivated into many forms, including the [[turnip]] (a [[root vegetable]]), [[komatsuna]], [[Chinese cabbage]], [[bomdong]], [[Bok_choy|pak choi / bok choy]], and [[rapini]]. Its domesticated forms include turnips and leafy greens, such as bok choy and napa cabbage. The oilseed types are grown for food and industrial uses. Genetic studies indicate that ''B. rapa'' was one of the earliest domesticated brassicas, with turnip-like forms arising first and additional [[Polymorphism (biology)|morphotypes]] developing independently across Eurasia. Wild, feral, and cultivated populations are found worldwide, making the species important agriculturally, economically, and ecologically.<ref name="McAlvay et al 2021" /> 

[[Rapeseed oil]] is a general term for oil from some ''Brassica'' species. Food grade oil made from the seed of low-[[erucic acid]] Canadian-developed strains is also called [[canola oil]], while non-food oil is called [[colza oil]].<ref name=USDA /> Canola oil can be sourced from ''Brassica rapa'' and ''[[Brassica napus]]'', which are commonly grown in Canada, and ''[[Brassica juncea]]'', which is less common.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.canolacouncil.org/canola-encyclopedia/history-of-canola-seed-development|title=History of Canola Seed Development | Canola Encyclopedia}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Leiden University Library - Seikei Zusetsu vol. 21, page 014 - 菘 - Brassica rapa L., 1804.jpg|thumb|Illustration of ''Brassica rapa'' from the Japanese agricultural encyclopedia ''[[Seikei Zusetsu]].'']]
The geographic and genetic origins of ''B. rapa'' have been difficult to identify due to its long history of human cultivation, as well as difficulty finding ''Brassica'' seeds at archaeological sites. It is found in most parts of the world, and has returned to the wild many times as a [[feral plant]] or [[weed]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McAlvay |first1=Alex C |last2=Ragsdale |first2=Aaron P |last3=Mabry |first3=Makenzie E |last4=Qi |first4=Xinshuai |last5=Bird |first5=Kevin A |last6=Velasco |first6=Pablo |last7=An |first7=Hong |last8=Pires |first8=J Chris |last9=Emshwiller |first9=Eve |date=2021-07-29 |editor-last=Purugganan |editor-first=Michael |title=Brassica rapa Domestication: Untangling Wild and Feral Forms and Convergence of Crop Morphotypes |url=https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/38/8/3358/6261082 |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |language=en |volume=38 |issue=8 |pages=3358–3372 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msab108 |issn=1537-1719 |pmc=8321528 |pmid=33930151}}</ref> Recent genomic studies show that many “wild” populations found in Europe and the Americas are actually feral descendants of cultivated plants, while actual wild populations appear to be from regions such as the [[Caucasus]] and [[Central Asia]].<ref name="McAlvay et al 2021" /> 

Genetic sequencing and environmental modeling have indicated that ancestral ''B. rapa'' likely originated 4000 to 6000 years ago in the [[Hindu Kush]] area of Central Asia, and had three sets of [[chromosomes]], providing the genetic potential for a diversity of form, flavor, and growth. Domestication has produced modern vegetables and oil-seed crops, all with two sets of chromosomes.<ref name="Tarlach2021">{{cite web |last1=Tarlach |first1=Gemma |title=The Deep Roots of the Vegetable That 'Took Over the World' |url=https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/brassica-rapa-vegetable-domestication |website=Atlas Obscura |date=11 June 2021 |access-date=30 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="McAlvay et al 2021">{{cite journal |last1=McAlvay |first1=Alex C |last2=Ragsdale |first2=Aaron P |last3=Mabry |first3=Makenzie E |last4=Qi |first4=Xinshuai |last5=Bird |first5=Kevin A |last6=Velasco |first6=Pablo |last7=An |first7=Hong |last8=Pires |first8=J Chris |last9=Emshwiller |first9=Eve |title=Brassica rapa Domestication: Untangling Wild and Feral Forms and Convergence of Crop Morphotypes |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |date=2021 |volume=38 |issue=8 |pages=3358–3372 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msab108|pmid=33930151 |pmc=8321528 }}</ref> 

Oilseed [[subspecies]] (subsp. ''oleifera'') of ''Brassica rapa'' may have been domesticated several times from the [[Mediterranean]] to [[India]], starting as early as 2000 BC.<ref name="sanderson">{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Sanderson |first1=Helen|date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=72 |isbn=0415927463}}</ref> There are descriptions of ''B. rapa'' vegetables in Indian and Chinese documents from around 1000 BC.<ref name="Tarlach2021" />  

Edible turnips were possibly first cultivated in northern Europe, and were an important food in [[ancient Rome]].<ref name="sanderson" /> The turnip then spread east to China, and reached Japan by 700 AD.<ref name="sanderson" /> 

In the 18th century, the turnip and the oilseed-producing variants were thought to be different species by [[Carl Linnaeus]], who named them ''B. rapa'' and ''B. campestris''. Twentieth-century taxonomists found that the plants were [[Cross-fertilization|cross fertile]] and belonged to the same species. Since the turnip had been named first by Linnaeus, the name ''Brassica rapa'' was assigned to the plant in his work ''[[Species Plantarum]]''.<ref>{{cite book |publisher=Canola Council of Canada |editor-first1=Phil |editor-last=Thomas |chapter=Canola Varieties |title=Canola Growers Manual |year=2003 |chapter-url=http://www.canolacouncil.org/chapter2.aspx |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090712144055/http://www.canolacouncil.org/chapter2.aspx |archive-date=12 July 2009 }}</ref>

== Biology ==
''Brassica rapa'' is an annual to biennial member of the [[Brassicaceae|mustard]] family.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Islam |first1=Rabiul |last2=Howlett |first2=Brad G. |last3=Chapman |first3=Hazel |last4=Haque |first4=Md. Azizul |last5=Ahmad |first5=Masum |date=2022-03-01 |title=The value of insect pollination to yield of oilseed rape (Brassica rapa) in Bangladesh |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1226861521001710 |journal=Journal of Asia-Pacific Entomology |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=101844 |doi=10.1016/j.aspen.2021.11.005 |bibcode=2022JAsPE..2501844I |issn=1226-8615|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The wild and weedy forms typically have a slender [[taproot]] and a leafy rosette, whereas turnip forms form a swollen storage [[root]]. The stems are often upright and branched, and they usually grow to around 0.5–1.3 meters in height. The lower leaves are stalked and toothed or lobed, while the upper leaves are narrower. Most flowers have four yellow petals and, after flowering, they develop into narrow seed pods. Many forms of ''Brassica rapa'' can be differentiated by the presence of hairs on the stem and the type of fruit pod. 

''B. rapa'' can behave as a summer annual, winter annual, or biannual depending on the climate and management. It can grow in a wide variety of environments and soil types, and it is also common as an escaped plant. The species reproduces by [[seed]]. The mature seed pods can break open and release viable seeds into the surrounding area, which creates seed banks that germinate quickly (~1-3 days) in ideal soil temperatures. Like other brassicas, ''B. rapa'' contains secondary [[Metabolite|metabolites]] like [[Glucosinolate|glucosinolates]], which can influence the [[germination]] of neighboring plants and deter herbivores. The flowers supply plentiful pollen and nectar and are visited by a variety of insects, including bees and flies, which act as pollinators.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gulden |first1=R. H. |last2=Warwick |first2=S. I. |last3=Thomas |first3=A. G. |title=The Biology of Canadian Weeds. 137. Brassica napus L. and B. rapa L. |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/epdf/10.4141/CJPS07203 |access-date=2025-12-06 |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |date=2008 |volume=88 |issue=5 |pages=951–996 |language=en |doi=10.4141/cjps07203 |bibcode=2008CJPlS..88..951G }}</ref>  

''Brassica rapa'' is a [[diploid]] with a base chromosome number of 10. The estimated [[genome]] size is approximately 425 million base pairs. A near complete [[genome assembly]] of ''B. rapa'' was published in 2023 (Chiifu v4.0), with eight out of ten chromosomes assembled [[telomere-to-telomere]] with only two gaps.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Lei |last2=Liang |first2=Jianli |last3=Chen |first3=Haixu |last4=Zhang |first4=Zhicheng |last5=Wu |first5=Jian |last6=Wang |first6=Xiaowu |date=2023 |title=A near-complete genome assembly of Brassica rapa provides new insights into the evolution of centromeres |journal=Plant Biotechnology Journal |language=en |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=1022–1032 |doi=10.1111/pbi.14015 |doi-access=free |issn=1467-7652 |pmc=10106856 |pmid=36688739 |bibcode=2023PBioJ..21.1022Z }}</ref>

== Adaptation ==
''Brassica rapa'' is an extremely adaptable plant. It prefers moist soil that is well-drained at around 45-85°F, but it can also grow in heavy clay soils.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=USDA Plants Database |url=https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/BRRA |access-date=2025-12-16 |website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref> It tolerates a broad pH range from 4.8 to 8.5. Although it grows best in full sun, it can also succeed in moderate shade. If light and temperature conditions are not ideal, ''B. rapa'' seeds can delay germination until conditions are favorable. 

==Uses==
Cultivated varieties of ''B. rapa'' are consumed commonly as vegetables, such as turnip roots, napa cabbage, komatsuna, pak choi, and other leafy greens, particularly in East Asian, South Asian, and Mediterranean cuisines.<ref name="McAlvay et al 2021" /> The young leaves are a [[leaf vegetable]] eaten raw, while older leaves are typically cooked. The taproot and seeds can also be eaten raw, although the seeds contain an oil that can cause irritation for some people.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Benoliel|first=Doug|title=Northwest Foraging: The Classic Guide to Edible Plants of the Pacific Northwest|publisher=Skipstone|year=2011|isbn=978-1-59485-366-1|edition=Rev. and updated|location=Seattle, WA|pages=83–84|oclc=668195076}}</ref> Rapeseed oil from the plant is also used to make canola and colza oils.<ref name=":0" />

''B. rapa'' is also commonly used as a rotational cover crop for vegetables due to its ability to prevent erosion and deter disease.<ref name=":1" /> Because of their fast life-cycle and genetic diversity, the ''B. rapa'' cultivar [[Wisconsin Fast Plants]] is widely used in genetics and plant biology education.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wendell |first1=Douglas L. |last2=Pickard |first2=Dawn |date=2007 |title=Teaching human genetics with mustard: rapid cycling Brassica rapa (fast plants type) as a model for human genetics in the classroom laboratory |journal=CBE: Life Sciences Education |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=179–185 |doi=10.1187/cbe.07-02-0010 |issn=1931-7913 |pmc=1885900 |pmid=17548880}}</ref>

== Ecology and pollination ==
''Brassica rapa'' is an early-season nectar and pollen source for a wide range of insects. Numerous pollinators are attracted to its bright yellow flowers, including bees, flies, and butterflies. A common visitor, the small white butterfly (''[[Pieris rapae]]'') uses the plant both as a nectar source and as a host for larval feeding. Conversely, insect pollination is also very important to the plant; insect pollination of ''B. rapa'' leads to 30% more yield when compared to self-fertilizing controls.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Islam |first1=Rabiul |last2=Howlett |first2=Brad G. |last3=Chapman |first3=Hazel |last4=Haque |first4=Md. Azizul |last5=Ahmad |first5=Masum |date=2022-03-01 |title=The value of insect pollination to yield of oilseed rape (Brassica rapa) in Bangladesh |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1226861521001710 |journal=Journal of Asia-Pacific Entomology |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=101844 |doi=10.1016/j.aspen.2021.11.005 |bibcode=2022JAsPE..2501844I |issn=1226-8615|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Furthermore, ''B. rapa'' can undergo rapid genomic adaptations when selected on by bumblebees.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Frachon |first1=Léa |last2=Schiestl |first2=Florian P. |date=2024-01-09 |title=Rapid genomic evolution in Brassica rapa with bumblebee selection in experimental evolution |journal=BMC Ecology and Evolution |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=7 |doi=10.1186/s12862-023-02194-y |doi-access=free |issn=2730-7182 |pmc=10775529 |pmid=38195402}}</ref>
